paragraphs.heading: One year, two bands
paragraphs.text: A varve is the whole layer of sediment that settles in a single year on the bed of a lake or sea. In its classic form it is a pair of bands, one coarse and one fine, for each yearly cycle. The coarse band comes from spring, when stronger currents wash in bigger grains than the ones that drift down later in the year. Since every pair stands for one year, counting the pairs dates a sediment profile with high precision.

paragraphs.heading: Why they matter
paragraphs.text: The rock record holds many kinds of rhythmically layered deposits, and varves rank among the most important of them for studying how climate changed in the past. They also capture some of the smallest events that geologists can pick out in layered rock. A Swedish varve chronology, built from thousands of sites, now spans 13,200 varve years. As late as 2008 varves were judged too uncertain for long timescales, but by 2012 researchers at Lake Suigetsu had found missing layers by overlapping several cores and counting more carefully, stretching that record to 52,800 years.

paragraphs.heading: Where they can form
paragraphs.text: Varves form only in fresh or brackish water. In normal seawater the salt makes clay clump into coarse grains, so coarse particles settle all year round and the yearly bands become almost impossible to tell apart. Layering also needs an absence of bioturbation. For that reason varves commonly form in anoxic, oxygen-free conditions.

paragraphs.heading: Light summers, dark springs
paragraphs.text: In the classic lake varve, the pair is one light band and one dark band. The light band builds up in summer, when phytoplankton and other tiny organisms with shells or skeletons of silica or calcium carbonate die and sink to the bottom. This rain of dead organisms happens only in the warm months, when the lake is most productive. The dark band holds organic matter and fine particles carried in by spring floods of melted winter snow.

paragraphs.heading: A Swedish idea
paragraphs.text: The name comes from the Swedish word varv, whose meanings include 'circle', 'revolution' and 'in layers'. It first appeared in 1862 on the first map made by the Geological Survey of Sweden. While mapping for that survey, the geologist Gerard De Geer saw that banded sediments looked very like tree rings. He proposed that the coarse-fine pairs common in glacial lakes were yearly layers, and in the late 19th century he built the first varve chronology in Stockholm. In 1910 he gave the word its formal meaning: the whole of one year's layer.

paragraphs.heading: Matching layers far apart
paragraphs.text: By 1914 De Geer found he could match varve sequences over long distances by comparing changes in layer thickness and distinctive marker layers. The method was pushed too far: he and many co-workers drew false links between continents, which other researchers such as Ernst Antevs criticised. Varves can also record single events. In the Piànico–Sèllere Basin in the southern Alps, the detrital layer in each varve was used to trace 771 ancient floods over 9.3 thousand years during an interglacial period of the Pleistocene.
